Derivatives on Graphs for the Positive Calculus of Relations with Transitive Closure
Yoshiki Nakamura ORCID:0000-0003-4106-0408

Abstract
. We prove that the equational theory of the positive calculus of relations with transitive closure (PCoR*) is EXPSPACE-complete. Here, PCoR* terms consist of the following standard operators on binary relations: identity, empty, universality, union, intersection, composition, converse, and reflexive transitive closure (so, PCoR* terms subsume Kleene algebra and allegory terms as fragments). Additionally, we show that the equational theory of PCoR* extended with tests and nominals (in hybrid logic) is still EXPSPACE-complete; moreover, it is PSPACE-complete for its intersection-free fragment. To this end, we design derivatives on graphs by extending derivatives on words for regular expressions. The derivatives give a finite automata construction on path decompositions, like those on words. Because the equational theory has a linearly bounded pathwidth model property, we can decide the equational theory of PCoR* using these automata.

Introduction

We consider
the positive calculus of relations with transitive closure
(PCoR*)
[
pousPositiveCalculusRelations2018
]
:
the algebraic system on binary relations,
with the operators
\{\mathsf{1},\mathsf{0},\top,\mathbin{;},\mathbin{+},\mathbin{\cap},\_^{\smile},\_^{*}\}
of identity (
\mathsf{1}
), empty (
\mathsf{0}
), universality (
\top
), composition (
\mathbin{;}
), union (
\mathbin{+}
), intersection (
\mathbin{\cap}
), converse (
\_^{\smile}
), and reflexive transitive closure (
\_^{*}
);
so, PCoR* consist of the operators of Kleene algebra
\{\mathsf{1},\mathsf{0},\mathbin{;},\mathbin{+},\_^{*}\}

[
kleeneRepresentationEventsNerve1956
,
conwayRegularAlgebraFinite1971
,
kozenCompletenessTheoremKleene1991
]
, those of allegory
\{\mathsf{1},\mathbin{;},\mathbin{\cap},\_^{\smile}\}

[
freydCategoriesAllegories1990
]
,
and
\top
.
PCoR* terms without
\top
are sometimes called
Kleene allegory
terms
[
brunetPetriAutomataKleene2015
,
brunetPetriAutomata2017
,
nakamuraPartialDerivativesGraphs2017
]
.

If we added the complement operator (
\_^{-}
) to PCoR*, then we would obtain the calculus of relations
[
tarskiCalculusRelations1941
,
tarskiFormalizationSetTheory1987
]
with transitive closure
[
ngRelationAlgebrasTransitive1984
]
.
However, the equational theory of the calculus of relations is well-known undecidable
[
tarskiCalculusRelations1941
,
tarskiFormalizationSetTheory1987
]
.
The undecidability result holds even for the terms with the three operators
\{\mathbin{;},\mathbin{+},\_^{-}\}

[
hirschDecidabilityEquationalTheories2018
]
and moreover even with one variable
[
nakamuraUndecidabilityFO3Calculus2019
]
.
Also, in PCoR* with
\_^{-}
, even if the complement only applies to atomic terms (variables or constants), the equational theory is still undecidable
[
nakamuraExistentialCalculiRelations2023
]
.
In this paper, by excluding complement, we focus on
positive
fragments.
For Kleene algebras (with respect to binary relations), the equational theory coincides with the language equivalence problem of regular expressions (see,
e.g.
,
[
pousPositiveCalculusRelations2018
, Theorem 4]
), and thus the equational theory of Kleene algebras is decidable and PSPACE-complete, by the results on regular expressions
[
meyerEquivalenceProblemRegular1972
]
.
For representable allegories (with respect to binary relations), the equational theory coincides with the graph homomorphic equivalence problem via an encoding of terms as graphs
[
freydCategoriesAllegories1990
,
andrekaEquationalTheoryUnionfree1995
,
chandraOptimalImplementationConjunctive1977
]
,
and thus the equational theory of representable allegories is also decidable.
For the equational theory of PCoR*, Brunet and Pous extended the graph homomorphism characterizations above using graph languages
[
brunetPetriAutomataKleene2015
,
brunetPetriAutomata2017
]
.
By introducing Petri automata, which is an automata model for expressing graph languages,
they have shown that the equational theory of
identity-free Kleene lattices

\{\mathsf{0},\mathbin{;},\mathbin{+},\mathbin{\cap},\_^{+}\}
with respect to binary relations
[
andrekaEquationalTheoryKleene2011
]
is decidable and EXPSPACE-complete
[
brunetPetriAutomataKleene2015
,
brunetPetriAutomata2017
]
where
(\_^{+})
denotes the transitive closure operator.
However, the decidability and complexity for Kleene allegories (and PCoR*) were left open at LICS 2015
[
brunetPetriAutomataKleene2015
]
.

Our main contribution is to prove that the equational theory of PCoR* is still decidable and EXPSPACE-complete.
We first note that the equational theory has the treewidth at most
2
model property (
Proposition

6
) and the linearly bounded pathwidth model property (
Proposition

7
).
Thus, the decidability can be derived from the decidability of MSO over bounded treewidth structures
[
courcelleMonadicSecondorderLogic1988
,
courcelleMonadicSecondorderLogic1990
,
courcelleGraphStructureMonadic2012
]
.
However, the naive algorithm obtained from this fact has a non-elementary complexity (see
, for more comparisons to other systems related to PCoR*).
The EXPSPACE-hardness is shown by giving a reduction from the universality problem of regular expressions with intersection, which is EXPSPACE-complete
[
furerComplexityInequivalenceProblem1980
, Theorem 2]
.
(This was independently shown in
[
nakamuraPartialDerivativesGraphs2017
,
brunetPetriAutomata2017
]
.)

To obtain the EXPSPACE upper bound of the equational theory of PCoR*,
we use the idea of derivatives on words for regular expressions,
e.g.
, Brzozowski’s derivatives
[
brzozowskiDerivativesRegularExpressions1964
]
and Antimirov’s (partial) derivatives
[
antimirovPartialDerivativesRegular1996
,
bastosStateComplexityPartial2016
]
,
that are tools to obtain automata from regular expressions syntactically (we refer to the book
[
sakarovitchElementsAutomataTheory2009
]
, for more details of derivatives on words).
In this paper, we extend the derivatives from words to graphs.
To this end, we consider Kleene lattices
\{\mathsf{1},\mathsf{0},\mathbin{;},\mathbin{+},\mathbin{\cap},\_^{*}\}
, which is a core fragment of PCoR*,
and we extend the syntax of terms with
labels
for pointing multiple vertices on graphs (
Section

3
).
Thanks to this extension, similar to those on words, we can give derivatives on graphs/structures (
Section

4
).
Derivatives of labeled Kleene lattice terms can simulate left quotients of languages of runs (having a special form of DAG) (
Section

2.2.1
),
as with that derivatives of regular expressions can simulate left quotients of word languages.
Moreover, we show that our derivatives are decomposable on path decompositions (
).
Namely, from derivatives on (small) pre-glued graphs, we can compute the derivative on the (large) glued graph (in this sense, our approach can be viewed as a variant of the Feferman–Vaught decomposition theorem
[
makowskyAlgorithmicUsesFeferman2004
,
courcelleGraphStructureMonadic2012
]
).
Thanks to this decomposition with the linearly bounded pathwidth model property (
Proposition

7
),
we can obtain an automata construction for Kleene lattice terms (
).
Using this construction, we have that the equational theory of Kleene lattices with respect to relations is EXPSPACE-complete (
).
Moreover, we show that on our automata construction, we can give encodings of the following operators: universality (
\top
), converse (
\_^{\smile}
), tests in Kleene algebra with tests (KAT), and nominals in hybrid logic.
Thus, the equational theory of PCoR* is EXPSPACE-complete (
), and moreover,
the equational theory of PCoR* with tests and nominals is EXPSPACE-complete (
).
Additionally, if the intersection width
[
gollerPDLIntersectionConverse2009
]
is fixed (particularly, if
\cap
does not occur),
the equational theory of PCoR* with tests and nominals is PSPACE-complete (
).

Differences with the version at LICS 2017

This is a revised and extended version of the paper
[
nakamuraPartialDerivativesGraphs2017
]
, presented at the 32nd Annual ACM/IEEE Symposium on Logic in Computer Science (LICS 2017).
The differences from the conference version are as follows.

•

To express bounded pathwidth structures,
we use a graph gluing operator (
\odot
)
[
bojanczykDefinabilityEqualsRecognizability2016
]
, instead of “Sequential Graph Constructing Procedures” (SGCPs)
[
nakamuraPartialDerivativesGraphs2017
]
.
Roughly speaking,
SGCPs enumerate “normalized” (but complete to generate all structures of pathwidth at most
k
) path decompositions of width at most
k
,
but combinations of the gluing operator enumerate
all
path decompositions of width at most
k
.
Due to this,
the alphabet size, here, the number of structures of size at most
k+1
, is large, naively, but we can reduce it (see
).
Thanks to this separation of concerns, our formalizations are significantly simplified without changing the essence.

•

Thanks to the above, we can easily encode some additional operators,
e.g.
, top (
\top
), converse (
\_^{\smile}
), tests in Kleene algebra with tests, and nominals in hybrid logic (
and
).
In the body of this paper, relying on these encodings, instead of PCoR* terms,
we mainly consider Kleene lattice terms—PCoR* terms with neither
\top
nor
\_^{\smile}
.
This separation also slightly simplifies our formalizations.

•

We use runs (defined in
Section

2.2.1
) instead of “simple graphs” in
[
nakamuraPartialDerivativesGraphs2017
]
.
Because each vertex of runs precisely has one fun-in and one fun-out,
we can more easily define left quotients,
cf.

[
nakamuraPartialDerivativesGraphs2017
]
.
Our runs are essentially those of branching automata by Lodaya and Weil
[
lodayaSeriesparallelPosetsAlgebra1998
,
lodayaSeriesParallelLanguages2000
,
lodayaRationalityAlgebrasSeries2001
]
without minor changes.

•

We point out an error of
[
nakamuraPartialDerivativesGraphs2017
, Section IV]
in
.
We give a counterexample that
the decomposition rules corresponding to the argument in
[
nakamuraPartialDerivativesGraphs2017
, Lemma IV.10]
are not complete (
cf.

), due to one-way reading.
To avoid this problem, we use two-way alternating finite automata (2AFAs), not one-way.

Outline

In
Section

2
, we give basic definitions, including PCoR* terms and Kleene lattice terms (KL terms).
In
Section

3
, we extend KL terms with labels.
In
Section

4
, we define derivatives on structures (graphs without interfaces) for labeled KL terms.
In
, we give an automata construction using the derivatives.
We then have that the equational theory of KL terms is EXPSPACE-complete.
In
, we give encodings of additional operators in our automata construction.
Consequently, the equational theory of PCoR* terms with tests and nominals is also EXPSPACE-complete.
In
, we prove the decomposition theorem for the derivatives, which is the key to our automata construction in
.
In
, we conclude this paper with related and future work.

2.
Preliminaries

We write
{\rm Nature}
for the set of non-negative integers.
For
l,r\in{\rm Nature}
, we write
[l,r]
for the set
\{i\in{\rm Nature}\mid l\leq i\leq r\}
.
For
n\in{\rm Nature}
, we abbreviate
[1,n]
to
[n]
.
For a set
X
, we write

\#X
for the cardinality of
X
and
\wp(X)
for the power set of
X
.
We use
\uplus
to denote that the union
\cup
is disjoint.

Word languages

We write
wv
for the concatenation of words
w
and
v
.
We write
\varepsilon
for the
empty word
.
For a set
X
of
letters
, we write
X^{*}
for the set of
words
over
X
.
A
language
over
X
is a subset of
X^{*}
.
We use
w,v
to denote words and use
\mathcal{L},\mathcal{K}
to denote languages.
For languages
\mathcal{L},\mathcal{K}\subseteq X^{*}
, the
concatenation

\mathcal{L}\mathbin{;}\mathcal{K}
,
the
n
-th iteration

\mathcal{L}^{n}
(where
n\in{\rm Nature}
),
the
Kleene plus

\mathcal{L}^{+}
, and
the
Kleene star

\mathcal{L}^{*}
are defined by:

\displaystyle\mathcal{L}\mathbin{;}\mathcal{K}

\displaystyle\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-3.0556pt\raisebox{5.64096pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\triangle$}}\hskip-3.0556pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\{wv\mid w\in\mathcal{L}\land v\in\mathcal{K}\},\hskip-1.00006pt

\displaystyle\mathcal{L}^{n}

\displaystyle\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-3.0556pt\raisebox{5.64096pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\triangle$}}\hskip-3.0556pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\begin{cases}\mathcal{L}\mathbin{;}\mathcal{L}^{n-1}&(n\geq 1)\\
\{\varepsilon\}&(n=0)\end{cases},\hskip-1.00006pt

\displaystyle\mathcal{L}^{+}

\displaystyle\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-3.0556pt\raisebox{5.64096pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\triangle$}}\hskip-3.0556pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\bigcup_{n\geq 1}\mathcal{L}^{n},\hskip-1.00006pt

\displaystyle\mathcal{L}^{*}

\displaystyle\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-3.0556pt\raisebox{5.64096pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\triangle$}}\hskip-3.0556pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\bigcup_{n\geq 0}\mathcal{L}^{n}.

Binary relations

We write
\triangle_{A}
for the identity relation on a set
A
:
\triangle_{A}\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-3.0556pt\raisebox{5.64096pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\triangle$}}\hskip-3.0556pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\{\langle x,x\rangle\mid x\in A\}
.
For binary relations
R,S
on a set
B
, the
composition

R\mathbin{;}S
, the
converse

R^{\smile}
, the
n
-th iteration

R^{n}
(where
n\in{\rm Nature}
), the
transitive closure

R^{+}
, and the
reflexive transitive closure

R^{*}
are defined by:

\displaystyle R\mathbin{;}S

\displaystyle\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-3.0556pt\raisebox{5.64096pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\triangle$}}\hskip-3.0556pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\{\langle x,z\rangle\mid\exists y,\ \langle x,y\rangle\in R\land\langle y,z\rangle\in S\},

\displaystyle R^{\smile}

\displaystyle\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-3.0556pt\raisebox{5.64096pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\triangle$}}\hskip-3.0556pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\{\langle x,y\rangle\mid\langle y,x\rangle\in R\},

\displaystyle R^{n}

\displaystyle\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-3.0556pt\raisebox{5.64096pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\triangle$}}\hskip-3.0556pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\begin{cases}R\mathbin{;}R^{n-1}&(n\geq 1)\\
\triangle_{B}&(n=0)\end{cases},

\displaystyle R^{+}

\displaystyle\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-3.0556pt\raisebox{5.64096pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\triangle$}}\hskip-3.0556pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\bigcup_{n\geq 1}R^{n},\qquad R^{*}\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-3.0556pt\raisebox{5.64096pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\triangle$}}\hskip-3.0556pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\bigcup_{n\geq 0}R^{n}.

Graphs with bi-interface

We consider graphs with bi-interface, inspired by
[
bojanczykDefinabilityEqualsRecognizability2016
, bi-interface graphs]
[
bonchiRewritingModuloSymmetric2016
, symmetric monoidal structures]
.
Interfaces are used to define the series composition (
Section

2
).
Let
A
be a set with a map
\mathrm{\mathop{ty}}\colon A\to{\rm Nature}^{2}
; we also let
\mathrm{\mathop{ty}}_{\mathsf{1}}
and
\mathrm{\mathop{ty}}_{\mathsf{2}}
be such that
\mathrm{\mathop{ty}}(a)=\langle\mathrm{\mathop{ty}}_{\mathsf{1}}(a),\mathrm{\mathop{ty}}_{\mathsf{2}}(a)\rangle
for each
a\in A
.
For
n,m\in{\rm Nature}
, a
graph

G
over
A
(with
\langle n,m\rangle
-interface) is a tuple

\langle|G|,\{a^{G}\}_{a\in A},\mathsf{1}_{1}^{G},\dots,\mathsf{1}_{n}^{G},\mathsf{2}_{1}^{G},\dots,\mathsf{2}_{m}^{G}\rangle
, where

•

|G|
is a (possibly empty) set;

•

a^{G}\subseteq|G|^{\mathrm{\mathop{ty}}_{1}(a)+\mathrm{\mathop{ty}}_{2}(a)}
is a
(\mathrm{\mathop{ty}}_{1}(a)+\mathrm{\mathop{ty}}_{2}(a))
-ary relation for each
a\in A
;

•

\mathsf{1}_{l}^{G}\in|G|
is the
l
-th
source
vertex for each
l\in[n]
;

•

\mathsf{2}_{r}^{G}\in|G|
is the
r
-th
target
vertex for each
r\in[m]
.

Particularly when
n=m=0
, we say that
G
is a graph without interfaces or
G
has no interfaces.
Note that, if
|G|=\emptyset
, then
n=m=0
.
We let
\mathrm{\mathop{ty}}(G)\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-3.0556pt\raisebox{5.64096pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\triangle$}}\hskip-3.0556pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\langle\mathrm{\mathop{ty}}_{1}(G),\mathrm{\mathop{ty}}_{2}(G)\rangle\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-3.0556pt\raisebox{5.64096pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\triangle$}}\hskip-3.0556pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\langle n,m\rangle
.
We often abbreviate
\mathsf{1}_{1}^{G}
to
\mathsf{1}^{G}
and
\mathsf{2}_{1}^{G}
to
\mathsf{2}^{G}
, respectively.

Let
G
and
H
be graphs over a set
A
with
\langle n,m\rangle
-interface.
We say that a map
f\colon|G|\to|H|
is a
graph homomorphism
from
G
to
H
, written
f\colon G\longrightarrow H
, if
(1) for each
a\in A
and
x_{1},\dots,x_{p}\in|G|
,
if
\langle x_{1},\dots,x_{p}\rangle\in a^{G}
, then
\langle f(x_{1}),\dots,f(x_{p})\rangle\in a^{H}
,
(2) for each
l\in[n]
,
f(\mathsf{1}_{l}^{G})=\mathsf{1}_{l}^{H}
, and
(3) for each
r\in[m]
,
f(\mathsf{2}_{r}^{G})=\mathsf{2}_{r}^{H}
.
Particularly, we say that
f
is a
graph isomorphism
from
G
to
H
, written
f\colon G\cong H
, if

f
is a bijective graph homomorphism from
G
to
H
, and
for each
a\in A
and
x_{1},\dots,x_{p}\in|G|
,

\langle x_{1},\dots,x_{p}\rangle\in a^{G}
iff
\langle f(x_{1}),\dots,f(x_{p})\rangle\in a^{H}
.
We write
G\longrightarrow H
(resp.
G\cong H
) if there is some
f\colon G\longrightarrow H

(resp.
f\colon G\cong H
).
In the sequel, we identify two graphs if there is a graph isomorphism between them (except for structures; see
Section

3.1
);
we write
G=H
when
G\cong H
.

For instance, when
A
is the set
\{a,\mathtt{f},\mathtt{j}\}
with
\mathrm{\mathop{ty}}(a)=\langle 1,1\rangle
,
\mathrm{\mathop{ty}}(\mathtt{f})=\langle 1,2\rangle
, and
\mathrm{\mathop{ty}}(\mathtt{j})=\langle 2,1\rangle

and the graph
G
is given by
|G|=\{1,2,3,4\}
,
a^{G}=\{\langle 1,2\rangle\}
,
\mathtt{f}^{G}=\{\langle 1,2,3\rangle\}
,
\mathtt{j}^{G}=\{\langle 2,3,4\rangle\}
,
\mathrm{\mathop{ty}}(G)=\langle 1,1\rangle
,

\mathsf{1}^{G}_{1}=1
, and
\mathsf{2}^{G}_{1}=4
,
we depict
G
as the figure on the left-hand side.
Here, we will use the symbols
\mathtt{f}
and
\mathtt{j}
as special constants (
Section

2.2.1
).
For notational simplicity, we often omit vertex labels and some “
1
” labels as the right-hand side.

Each
\mathsf{1}^{n}
is an
empty
graph and the graph
\mathsf{1}^{0}
is the
null
graph.
Each
\mathsf{1}^{n}
is the left identity element with respect to
\diamond
on graphs
G
with
\langle n,m\rangle
-interface, that is
\mathsf{1}^{n}\diamond G=G
.
The right identity element is given by
\mathsf{1}^{m}
, i.e.,
G\diamond\mathsf{1}^{m}=G
.
The identity element with respect to
\parallel
on graphs with
\langle n,m\rangle
-interface is given by
\mathsf{1}^{0}
, i.e.,

\mathsf{1}^{0}\parallel G=G\parallel\mathsf{1}^{0}=G
.

Pathwidth and treewidth

We recall the notions of the pathwidth and treewidth of structures
[
courcelleGraphStructureMonadic2012
, Definition 9.12]
,
which are defined based on the pathwidth
[
robertsonGraphMinorsExcluding1983
]
(see also,
e.g.
,
[
bodlaenderPartialArboretumGraphs1998
, Theorem 2]
[
bojanczykDefinabilityEqualsRecognizability2016
, Lemma 4.6]
for alternative characterizations) and the treewidth
[
robertsonGraphMinorsII1986
]
for graphs.
Below, for graphs with bi-interface, we use a slightly generalized definition, based on
[
courcelleGraphStructureMonadic2012
, Definition 2.5.3]
for treewidth and
[
nakamuraPartialDerivativesGraphs2017
]
for pathwidth (these definitions will be useful in the constructions in
4
and
3
, while we will always consider structures (graphs without interfaces)).
For a graph
G
(with bi-interface),
a
path decomposition
of
G
is a sequence
\vec{H}=H_{1}\dots H_{n}
of finite graphs such that

•

|G|=\bigcup_{i\in[n]}|H_{i}|
and
a^{G}=\bigcup_{i\in[n]}a^{H_{i}}
for each
a\in A
;

•

|H_{i}|\cap|H_{k}|\subseteq|H_{j}|\mbox{ for all $1\leq i\leq j\leq k\leq n$}
;

•

each source vertex of
G
is in
|H_{1}|

and each target vertex of
G
is in
|H_{n}|
.

The
width
of
\vec{H}
is
\max_{i\in[n]}(\#|H_{i}|-1)
.
The
pathwidth

\pw(G)
of a graph
G
is the minimum width among path decompositions of
G
.
Each element of
\vec{H}
is called a
bag
.

Similarly, for a graph
G
,
a
tree decomposition
of
G
is a finite rooted tree
\vec{H}=\{H_{w}\}_{w\in\Gamma}
of graphs, where
\Gamma\subseteq{\rm Nature}^{*}
is a finite and prefix-closed (
ww^{\prime}\in\Gamma
implies
w\in\Gamma
) set, such that

•

|G|=\bigcup_{w\in\Gamma}|H_{w}|
and
a^{G}=\bigcup_{w\in\Gamma}a^{H_{w}}
for each
a\in A
;

•

|H_{w}|\cap|H_{u}|\subseteq|H_{v}|
for all

w,v,u\in\Gamma
such that
v
is on the unique path between
w
and
u

(i.e.,
v
satisfies
\mathsf{LCA}(w,u)\preceq_{\mathrm{pref}}v\preceq_{\mathrm{pref}}w
or
\mathsf{LCA}(w,u)\preceq_{\mathrm{pref}}v\preceq_{\mathrm{pref}}u
where
w^{\prime}\preceq_{\mathrm{pref}}v^{\prime}
denotes that
w^{\prime}
is a prefix of
v^{\prime}
and
\mathsf{LCA}(w,u)
denotes the maximal common prefix word (i.e., the least common ancestor) of
w
and
u
);

•

each source vertex and each target vertex of
G
is in the root
|H_{\varepsilon}|
.

The
width
of
\vec{H}
is
\max_{w\in\Gamma}(\#|H_{w}|-1)
.
The
treewidth

\tw(G)
of a graph
G
is the minimum width among tree decompositions of
G
.
Each element of
\vec{H}
is called a
bag
.

Particularly when
G
has no interfaces,
the pathwidth/treewidth of a graph
G
coincide with those of its Gaifman graph (i.e., the graph
\langle|G|,E\rangle
where
E
is the binary relation
\bigcup_{a\in A}\bigcup_{\langle x_{1},\dots,x_{k}\rangle\in a^{G}}\{\langle x_{i},x_{j}\rangle\mid i,j\in[k]\land x_{i}\neq x_{j}\}

[
ebbinghausFiniteModelTheory1995
, p. 26]
), respectively.

Remark 1
.

By definition, the number of bags is finite; this is sufficient in this paper as we are mainly interested in finite structures (thanks to the
Proposition

5
).

2.1.
PCoR*: The Positive Calculus of Relations with Transitive Closure

We consider the positive calculus of relations with transitive closure (PCoR*).
We use
\Sigma
to denote a set of
variables
.
The set of
PCoR* terms
over
\Sigma
is defined as the set of terms over the signature
\{\mathsf{1}_{(0)},\mathsf{0}_{(0)},\top_{(0)},\mathbin{;}_{(2)},\mathbin{+}_{(2)},\mathbin{\cap}_{(2)},\_^{\smile}_{(1)},\_^{*}_{(1)}\}
and the variable set
\Sigma
:

\displaystyle t,s,{u}\;\Coloneqq\;a\mid\mathsf{1}\mid\mathsf{0}\mid\top\mid t\mathbin{;}s\mid t\mathbin{+}s\mid t\mathbin{\cap}s\mid t^{\smile}\mid t^{*}.

(
a\in\Sigma
)

We often abbreviate
t\mathbin{;}s
to
ts
.
We use parentheses in ambiguous situations (where
\mathbin{+}
,
\mathbin{;}
, and
\cap
are left-associative).
We write
\sum_{i=1}^{n}t_{i}
for the term
\mathsf{0}\mathbin{+}t_{1}\mathbin{+}\dots\mathbin{+}t_{n}
,
write
\bigcompo_{i=1}^{n}t_{i}
for the term
\mathsf{1}\mathbin{;}t_{1}\mathbin{;}\dots\mathbin{;}t_{n}
,
write
t^{n}
for the term
\bigcompo_{i=1}^{n}t
,
and write
t^{+}
for the term
tt^{*}
.

An
equation

t=s
is a pair of PCoR* terms.
The
inequation

t\leq s
abbreviates the equation
t\mathbin{+}s=s
.

For a PCoR* term
t
, the
size

\|t\|
is the number of symbols occurring in
t
:

\displaystyle\|a\|

\displaystyle\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-3.0556pt\raisebox{5.64096pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\triangle$}}\hskip-3.0556pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}1\mbox{ for $a\in\Sigma\cup\{\mathsf{1},\mathsf{0},\top\}$},

\displaystyle\|t^{\mathbin{\heartsuit}}\|

\displaystyle\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-3.0556pt\raisebox{5.64096pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\triangle$}}\hskip-3.0556pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}1+\|t\|\mbox{ for $\mathbin{\heartsuit}\in\{\smile,*\}$},

\displaystyle\|t\mathbin{\heartsuit}s\|

\displaystyle\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-3.0556pt\raisebox{5.64096pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\triangle$}}\hskip-3.0556pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}1+\|t\|+\|s\|\mbox{ for $\mathbin{\heartsuit}\in\{\mathbin{;},\mathbin{+},\mathbin{\cap}\}$.}

Additionally, the
intersection width

\iw(t)

[
gollerPDLIntersectionConverse2009
]
is defined as follows:

\displaystyle\iw(a)

\displaystyle\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-3.0556pt\raisebox{5.64096pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\triangle$}}\hskip-3.0556pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}1\mbox{ for $a\in\Sigma\cup\{\mathsf{1},\mathsf{0},\top\}$},

\displaystyle\iw(t^{\mathbin{\heartsuit}})

\displaystyle\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-3.0556pt\raisebox{5.64096pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\triangle$}}\hskip-3.0556pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\iw(t)\mbox{ for $\mathbin{\heartsuit}\in\{\smile,*\}$},

\displaystyle\iw(t\mathbin{\heartsuit}s)

\displaystyle\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-3.0556pt\raisebox{5.64096pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\triangle$}}\hskip-3.0556pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\max(\iw(t),\iw(s))\mbox{ for $\mathbin{\heartsuit}\in\{\mathbin{;},\mathbin{+}\}$},

\displaystyle\iw(t\mathbin{\cap}s)

\displaystyle\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-3.0556pt\raisebox{5.64096pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\triangle$}}\hskip-3.0556pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\iw(t)+\iw(s).

For instance,
\iw(a\mathbin{\cap}b\mathbin{\cap}c\mathbin{\cap}d)=4
and
\iw((a\mathbin{\cap}b)\mathbin{;}(a\mathbin{\cap}c)\mathbin{;}(a\mathbin{\cap}d))=2
.

Proposition 2
.

For all PCoR* terms
t
, we have
\iw(t)\leq\|t\|
.

Proof 2.1
.

By easy induction on
t
.

2.1.1.
Semantics: relational models

A
structure (of binary relations)
is a non-empty graph without interfaces over the set
\Sigma
with
\mathrm{\mathop{ty}}(a)=\langle 1,1\rangle
for
a\in\Sigma
.
We use
\mathfrak{A},\mathfrak{B}
to denote a structure.
Let
\mathfrak{A}
be a structure.
For a PCoR* term
t
,
the
semantics

\llbracket t\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}\subseteq|\mathfrak{A}|^{2}
is defined as follows:

\displaystyle\llbracket a\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-3.0556pt\raisebox{5.64096pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\triangle$}}\hskip-3.0556pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}a^{\mathfrak{A}},\qquad\llbracket\mathsf{1}\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-3.0556pt\raisebox{5.64096pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\triangle$}}\hskip-3.0556pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\triangle_{|\mathfrak{A}|},\qquad\llbracket\mathsf{0}\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-3.0556pt\raisebox{5.64096pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\triangle$}}\hskip-3.0556pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\emptyset,\qquad\llbracket\top\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-3.0556pt\raisebox{5.64096pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\triangle$}}\hskip-3.0556pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}|\mathfrak{A}|^{2},\qquad\llbracket t\mathbin{;}s\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-3.0556pt\raisebox{5.64096pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\triangle$}}\hskip-3.0556pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\llbracket t\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}\mathbin{;}\llbracket s\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}},

\displaystyle\llbracket t\mathbin{+}s\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-3.0556pt\raisebox{5.64096pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\triangle$}}\hskip-3.0556pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\llbracket t\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}\cup\llbracket s\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}},\qquad\llbracket t\mathbin{\cap}s\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-3.0556pt\raisebox{5.64096pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\triangle$}}\hskip-3.0556pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\llbracket t\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}\cap\llbracket s\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}},\qquad\llbracket t^{\smile}\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-3.0556pt\raisebox{5.64096pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\triangle$}}\hskip-3.0556pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\llbracket t\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}^{\smile},\qquad\llbracket t^{*}\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-3.0556pt\raisebox{5.64096pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\triangle$}}\hskip-3.0556pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\llbracket t\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}^{*}.

We write
\mathsf{REL}
for the class of all structures.
For
\mathcal{C}\subseteq\mathsf{REL}
,
we write
\mathcal{C}\models t=s
if
\llbracket t\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}=\llbracket s\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}
for all
\mathfrak{A}\in\mathcal{C}
.
In the sequel, we consider the
equational theory
with respect to
\mathsf{REL}
.
For instance, the following equations hold with respect to
\mathsf{REL}
:

\displaystyle(t^{*}s^{*})^{*}=(t\mathbin{+}s)^{*}

(1)

\displaystyle t^{*}=(tt)^{*}(\mathsf{1}\mathbin{+}t)

(2)

\displaystyle t(s\mathbin{\cap}{u})\leq(ts)\mathbin{\cap}(t{u})

(3)

\displaystyle(ts)\mathbin{\cap}{u}\leq(t\mathbin{\cap}({u}s^{\smile}))s

(4)

\displaystyle t^{+}\mathbin{\cap}\mathsf{1}\leq(tt)^{+}

(5)

\displaystyle(t\mathbin{\cap}s^{\smile})^{+}\mathbin{\cap}\mathsf{1}\leq(t\mathbin{\cap}s^{+})^{+}

(6)

Notably,
the equational theory of PCoR* contains that of Kleene algebras
\{\mathsf{1},\mathsf{0},\mathbin{;},\mathbin{+},\_^{*}\}

[
kozenCompletenessTheoremKleene1991
]
(such as
Equations

1
and
2
)
and that of allegories
\{\mathsf{1},\mathbin{;},\mathbin{\cap},\_^{\smile}\}

[
freydCategoriesAllegories1990
,
pousAllegoriesDecidabilityGraph2018
]
(such as
Equation

3
(the semi-distributive law over
\cap
) and
Equation

4
(the modularity law));
see also
[
bloomNotesEquationalTheories1995
,
brunetAlgorithmsKleeneAlgebra2016
]
for Kleene algebras with converse
\{\mathsf{1},\mathsf{0},\mathbin{;},\mathbin{+},\_^{*},\_^{\smile}\}

and
[
andrekaEquationalTheoryKleene2011
,
doumaneCompletenessIdentityfreeKleene2018
]
for identity-free Kleene lattices
\{\mathsf{0},\mathbin{;},\mathbin{+},\mathbin{\cap},\_^{+}\}
.

Equation

5

[
pousPositiveCalculusRelations2018
, p. 14]
and
Equation

6
are non-trivial equations having transitive closure and intersection.

Proposition 3
.

For all PCoR* terms
t
and
G\in\mathcal{G}(t)
, we have
\tw(G)\leq 2
.

Proof 2.2

(Proof (Corollary of
[
bodlaenderPartialArboretumGraphs1998
, Theorem 41]
))
.

By induction on
\{\mathbin{;},\mathbin{\cap}\}
-terms,
we have that every series-parallel graph (with one source and one target) has some tree decomposition of width
2

[
bodlaenderPartialArboretumGraphs1998
, Theorem 41]
.
Similar to this, by induction on PCoR* terms
t
,
each graph
G\in\mathcal{G}(t)
has some tree decomposition of width
2
.

Proposition 4
.

For all PCoR* terms
t
and
G\in\mathcal{G}(t)
, we have
\pw(G)\leq\iw(t)
.

Proof 2.3
.

Similar to the above, by easy induction on
t
,
each graph
G\in\mathcal{G}(t)

has some path decomposition
\vec{H}=H_{1}\dots H_{n}
of width
\iw(t)

(where the source vertex is in
|H_{1}|
and the target vertex is in
|H_{n}|
).

In this paper, we use the graph languages above as an alternative semantics.
Let
\mathfrak{A}
be a structure.
For
x,y\in|\mathfrak{A}|
,
we write
\mathsf{G}(\mathfrak{A},x,y)
for the graph defined by
\langle|\mathfrak{A}|,\{\llbracket a\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}\}_{a\in\Sigma},x,y\rangle
.
For a graph
H
and a set
\mathcal{G}
of graphs,
we define
\llbracket H\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}
and
\llbracket\mathcal{G}\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}
as follows:

\displaystyle\llbracket H\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}

\displaystyle\;\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-3.0556pt\raisebox{5.64096pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\triangle$}}\hskip-3.0556pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\;\{\langle x,y\rangle\mid H\longrightarrow\mathsf{G}(\mathfrak{A},x,y)\},

\displaystyle\llbracket\mathcal{G}\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}\;\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-3.0556pt\raisebox{5.64096pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\triangle$}}\hskip-3.0556pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\;\bigcup_{H\in\mathcal{G}}\llbracket H\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}.

We then have the following.

{propC}
[
[
andrekaEquationalTheoryKleene2011
, Lemma 2.1 and 2.2]
(for PCoR* without
\top
),
[
brunetPetriAutomata2017
, Lemma 2.3]
(for PCoR*)]
Let
\mathfrak{A}
be a structure.
For all PCoR* terms
t
, we have
\llbracket t\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}=\llbracket\mathcal{G}(t)\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}
.

using distributivity of
\mathbin{;}
,
\mathbin{\cap}
, and
\_^{\smile}

As a corollary of
Section

2.1.2
, we also have the following bounded model property.

Proposition 5

(Graph language bounded model property)
.

For all PCoR* terms
t,s
,

\mathsf{REL}\models t\leq s\;\iff\;\{\mathfrak{A}\mid\exists x,y\in|\mathfrak{A}|,\mathsf{G}(\mathfrak{A},x,y)\in\mathcal{G}(t)\}\models t\leq s.

Proof 2.5
.

(
\Longrightarrow
):
Trivial.
(
\Longleftarrow
):
We prove the contraposition.
Assume
\langle x,y\rangle\in\llbracket t\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}\setminus\llbracket s\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}
for some
\mathfrak{A}\in\mathsf{REL}
and
x,y\in|\mathfrak{A}|
.
By
Section

2.1.2
,

G^{\prime}\longrightarrow\mathsf{G}(\mathfrak{A},x,y)
for some
G^{\prime}\in\mathcal{G}(t)
, and

H\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 3.75pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{\longrightarrow}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 3.75pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{\longrightarrow}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.625pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{\longrightarrow}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.875pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{\longrightarrow}}}\mathsf{G}(\mathfrak{A},x,y)
for all
H\in\mathcal{G}(s)
.
Let
\mathfrak{B}
,
x^{\prime}
, and
y^{\prime}
be such that
\mathsf{G}(\mathfrak{B},x^{\prime},y^{\prime})=G^{\prime}
.
Since
G^{\prime}\longrightarrow\mathsf{G}(\mathfrak{B},x^{\prime},y^{\prime})
, we have
\langle x^{\prime},y^{\prime}\rangle\in\llbracket t\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{B}}
.
Also, by
\mathsf{G}(\mathfrak{B},x^{\prime},y^{\prime})\longrightarrow\mathsf{G}(\mathfrak{A},x,y)
,
we have
H\mathchoice{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 3.75pt\kern-5.27776pt$\displaystyle\not$\hss}{\longrightarrow}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 3.75pt\kern-5.27776pt$\textstyle\not$\hss}{\longrightarrow}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 2.625pt\kern-4.45831pt$\scriptstyle\not$\hss}{\longrightarrow}}}{\mathrel{\hbox to0.0pt{\kern 1.875pt\kern-3.95834pt$\scriptscriptstyle\not$\hss}{\longrightarrow}}}\mathsf{G}(\mathfrak{B},x^{\prime},y^{\prime})
for all
H\in\mathcal{G}(s)
,
and hence
\langle x^{\prime},y^{\prime}\rangle\not\in\llbracket s\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{B}}
.
Hence by
\mathsf{G}(\mathfrak{B},x^{\prime},y^{\prime})\in\mathcal{G}(t)
, this completes the proof.

For a class
\mathcal{C}\subseteq\mathsf{REL}
, we use the following notations:

\displaystyle\mathcal{C}_{\pw\leq k}

\displaystyle=\{\mathfrak{A}\in\mathcal{C}\mid\pw(\mathfrak{A})\leq k\},

\displaystyle\mathcal{C}_{\tw\leq k}

\displaystyle=\{\mathfrak{A}\in\mathcal{C}\mid\tw(\mathfrak{A})\leq k\}.

As a corollary of
Proposition

5
, we also have the following two model properties.

Proposition 6

(Treewidth at most
2
model property)
.

For all PCoR* terms
t,s
,

\mathsf{REL}\models t\leq s\;\iff\;\mathsf{REL}_{\tw\leq 2}\models t\leq s.

Proof 2.6
.

(
\Longrightarrow
):
Trivial.
(
\Longleftarrow
):
Because every graph of
\mathcal{G}(t)
has treewidth at most
2
(
Proposition

3
),
this direction is shown by
Proposition

5
.

Proposition 7

(Linearly bounded pathwidth model property)
.

For all PCoR* terms
t,s
,

\mathsf{REL}\models t\leq s\;\iff\;\mathsf{REL}_{\pw\leq\iw(t)}\models t\leq s.

Proof 2.7
.

(
\Longrightarrow
):
Trivial.
(
\Longleftarrow
):
Because every graph of
\mathcal{G}(t)
has pathwidth at most
\iw(t)
(
Proposition

4
),
this direction is shown by
Proposition

5
.

Note that we can easily translate the equational theory of PCoR* terms into the theory of monadic second-order logic (MSO) formulas
1
1

1

Precisely, with respect to binary relations, the expressive power of PCoR* is equivalent to that of three-variable existential positive logic with “variable-confined” monadic transitive closure
[
nakamuraExpressivePowerSuccinctness2022
]
.
as an analog of the standard translation from the equational theory of the calculus of relations into the theory of three-variable first-order logic formulas
[
tarskiCalculusRelations1941
]
.
Because the theory of MSO over bounded treewidth structures is decidable
[
courcelleMonadicSecondorderLogic1988
,
courcelleMonadicSecondorderLogic1990
,
courcelleGraphStructureMonadic2012
]
,

Proposition

6
(or
Proposition

7
) implies that the equational theory of PCoR* is decidable.
However, the naive algorithm obtained from the above has a non-elementary complexity.
We will show that the equational theory of PCoR* is EXPSPACE-complete (
).

Additionally, Brunet and Pous gave the following graph-theoretic characterization of the equational theory for PCoR*,
which generalizes the characterizations known for conjunctive queries
[
chandraOptimalImplementationConjunctive1977
]
, representable allegories
[
freydCategoriesAllegories1990
]
and union-free relation algebras
[
andrekaEquationalTheoryUnionfree1995
]
.

{propC}
[
[
brunetPetriAutomataKleene2015
,
brunetPetriAutomata2017
]
]
For all PCoR* terms
t,s
,

\mathsf{REL}\models t\leq s\;\iff\;\forall G\in\mathcal{G}(t),\exists H\in\mathcal{G}(s),H\longrightarrow G.

2.1.3.
Comparison to word languages

The word language
[t]_{\Sigma}
of a Kleene lattice term (i.e., terms over
\{\mathsf{1},\mathsf{0},\mathbin{;},\mathbin{+},\cap,\_^{*}\}
)
t
is the set of words over
\Sigma
defined as follows:

\displaystyle[a]_{\Sigma}

\displaystyle\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-3.0556pt\raisebox{5.64096pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\triangle$}}\hskip-3.0556pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\{a\}\mbox{ for $a\in\Sigma$},

\displaystyle[\mathsf{1}]_{\Sigma}

\displaystyle\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-3.0556pt\raisebox{5.64096pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\triangle$}}\hskip-3.0556pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\{\varepsilon\},

\displaystyle[\mathsf{0}]_{\Sigma}

\displaystyle\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-3.0556pt\raisebox{5.64096pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\triangle$}}\hskip-3.0556pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\emptyset,

\displaystyle[t\mathbin{+}s]_{\Sigma}

\displaystyle\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-3.0556pt\raisebox{5.64096pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\triangle$}}\hskip-3.0556pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}[t]_{\Sigma}\cup[s]_{\Sigma},

\displaystyle[t\mathbin{;}s]_{\Sigma}

\displaystyle\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-3.0556pt\raisebox{5.64096pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\triangle$}}\hskip-3.0556pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}[t]_{\Sigma}\mathbin{;}[s]_{\Sigma},

\displaystyle[t^{*}]_{\Sigma}

\displaystyle\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-3.0556pt\raisebox{5.64096pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\triangle$}}\hskip-3.0556pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}[t]_{\Sigma}^{*},

\displaystyle[t\mathbin{\cap}s]_{\Sigma}

\displaystyle\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-3.0556pt\raisebox{5.64096pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\triangle$}}\hskip-3.0556pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}[t]_{\Sigma}\cap[s]_{\Sigma}.

For Kleene algebra terms (i.e., terms over
\{\mathsf{1},\mathsf{0},\mathbin{;},\mathbin{+},\_^{*}\}
)
t
and
s
, the following is well-known (see,
e.g.
,
[
pousPositiveCalculusRelations2018
, Theorem 4]
):

\mathsf{REL}\models t\leq s
iff
[t]_{\Sigma}\subseteq[s]_{\Sigma}
.
This equivalence can be slightly strengthened as follows.

{propC}
[
[
nakamuraPartialDerivativesGraphs2017
,
brunetPetriAutomata2017
]
]
For all Kleene algebra terms
t
and Kleene lattice terms
s
, we have:

\mathsf{REL}\models t\leq s\;\iff\;[t]_{\Sigma}\subseteq[s]_{\Sigma}.

Proof 2.8
.

(In
[
nakamuraPartialDerivativesGraphs2017
, Theorem VI.3]
, this was shown via the tree unwinding technique in modal logic. The following is a simpler proof
[
brunetPetriAutomata2017
, Proposition 10.2]
based on the graph language characterization.)
For all Kleene lattice terms
s
and words
w\in\Sigma^{*}
, we have:

\exists H\in\mathcal{G}(s),H\longrightarrow\mathsf{G}(w)\;\iff\;w\in[s]_{\Sigma}

where
\mathsf{G}(w)
denotes the unique graph such that
\mathcal{G}(w)=\{\mathsf{G}(w)\}
.
It is shown by easy induction on
s
.
Thus by
Section

2.1.2
, this completes the proof.

Remark 8
.

The (word) language model
\mathsf{LANG}

[
bloomNotesEquationalTheories1995
,
andrekaEquationalTheoryKleene2011
,
brunetReversibleKleeneLattices2017
]
is another interesting model of PCoR* terms, where
the constant
\top
is interpreted as the universal language,
the unary operator
\_^{\smile}
is interpreted as the reverse of the language:
L^{\smile}\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-3.0556pt\raisebox{5.64096pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\triangle$}}\hskip-3.0556pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\{a_{n}\dots a_{2}a_{1}\mid a_{1}a_{2}\dots a_{n}\in L\}
,
and the other operators are defined based on the above
[\_]_{\Sigma}
.
In
\mathsf{LANG}
, each variable
x
may interpret not only
\{x\}
but also a (possibly non-singleton) language.
Notably for identity-free Kleene lattices,
the equational theory with respect to
\mathsf{LANG}
coincides with that with respect to
\mathsf{REL}

[
andrekaEquationalTheoryKleene2011
, Theorem 4.1]
.
However, for Kleene lattices and PCoR*, this coincidence is broken, e.g.,
Equations

4
,
5
and
6
are counterexamples.
For the equational theory of Kleene lattices (with complement),

\mathsf{LANG}
can be characterized as a subclass of (linearly ordered) (generalized) relational models
[
nakamuraFiniteRelationalSemantics2025
]
.

Remark 9
.

The restriction of
Section

2.1.3
is crucial.

Section

2.1.3
fails
when
\mathbin{\cap}
,
\top
, or
\_^{\smile}
occurs in
t
.
For instance, if
t=a\mathbin{\cap}b
and
s=\mathsf{0}
where
a\neq b
, then we have
[t]_{\Sigma}=[s]_{\Sigma}=\emptyset
but
a\mathbin{\cap}b\leq\mathsf{0}
does not hold with respect to
\mathsf{REL}
.

Section

2.1.3
also fails when
\top
or
\_^{\smile}
occurs in
s
(where
\top
expresses the universal language and
\_^{\smile}
expresses the reverse, according to
Remark

8
);
let us consider,
\mathsf{REL}\models a\leq a\top a
or
\mathsf{REL}\models a\leq aa^{\smile}a
.
In such cases, graph languages are needed (
Section

2.1.2
).

2.2.
Kleene lattice terms: a core fragment of PCoR* terms

In the sequel, we mainly consider Kleene lattice (KL) terms.
We say that a PCoR* term
t
is a
KL term
if
t
contains neither
\top
nor
\_^{\smile}
.
Namely, the set of KL terms is given by:

\displaystyle t,s,{u}\;\Coloneqq\;a\mid\mathsf{1}\mid\mathsf{0}\mid t\mathbin{;}s\mid t\mathbin{+}s\mid t\mathbin{\cap}s\mid t^{*}.

(
a\in\Sigma
)

2.2.1.
Second alternative semantics: run (DAG with vertices of one fan-in and one fan-out) languages

We consider run languages, which is a slightly modified semantics of graph languages.
This is inspired by the runs in branching automata
[
lodayaSeriesparallelPosetsAlgebra1998
,
lodayaSeriesParallelLanguages2000
,
lodayaRationalityAlgebrasSeries2001
]
.
We use the symbols
\mathtt{f}
and
\mathtt{j}
for expressing the forking and joining of runs, respectively.
Let
\Sigma_{\mathtt{f},\mathtt{j}}
be the set
\Sigma\cup\{\mathtt{f},\mathtt{j}\}
with the map
\mathrm{\mathop{ty}}
defined by:

\mathrm{\mathop{ty}}(a)=\langle 1,1\rangle\mbox{ for }a\in\Sigma
,

\mathrm{\mathop{ty}}(\mathtt{f})=\langle 1,2\rangle
, and

\mathrm{\mathop{ty}}(\mathtt{j})=\langle 2,1\rangle
.
A
run with
\langle n,m\rangle
-interface

G
is a graph with
\langle n,m\rangle
-interface over
\Sigma_{\mathtt{f},\mathtt{j}}
where

•

G
forms a directed acyclic graph (DAG), namely, the following holds:

\left(\bigcup_{a\in\Sigma_{\mathtt{f},\mathtt{j}}}\bigcup_{i\in[\mathrm{\mathop{ty}}_{1}(a)]}\bigcup_{j\in[\mathrm{\mathop{ty}}_{2}(a)]}\{\langle x_{i},y_{j}\rangle\mid\langle x_{1},\dots,x_{\mathrm{\mathop{ty}}_{1}(a)},y_{1},\dots,y_{\mathrm{\mathop{ty}}_{2}(a)}\rangle\in a^{G}\}\right)^{+}\cap\triangle_{|G|}=\emptyset.

•

\mathsf{in}_{G}(z)=\mathsf{out}_{G}(z)=1
for each
z\in|G|
, where

\displaystyle\mathsf{in}_{G}(z)

\displaystyle\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-3.0556pt\raisebox{5.64096pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\triangle$}}\hskip-3.0556pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\#\{l\in[n]\mid\mathsf{1}_{l}^{G}=z\}+\!\!\!\!\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}a\in\Sigma_{\mathtt{f},\mathtt{j}}\\
i\in[\mathrm{\mathop{ty}}_{1}(a)]\end{subarray}}\!\!\!\!\#\{\langle x_{1},\dots,x_{\mathrm{\mathop{ty}}_{1}(a)},y_{1},\dots,y_{\mathrm{\mathop{ty}}_{2}(a)}\rangle\!\in\!a^{G}\mid x_{i}=z\},

\displaystyle\mathsf{out}_{G}(z)

\displaystyle\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-3.0556pt\raisebox{5.64096pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\triangle$}}\hskip-3.0556pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\#\{r\in[m]\mid\mathsf{2}_{r}^{G}=z\}+\!\!\!\!\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}a\in\Sigma_{\mathtt{f},\mathtt{j}}\\
j\in[\mathrm{\mathop{ty}}_{2}(a)]\end{subarray}}\!\!\!\!\#\{\langle x_{1},\dots,x_{\mathrm{\mathop{ty}}_{1}(a)},y_{1},\dots,y_{\mathrm{\mathop{ty}}_{2}(a)}\rangle\!\in\!a^{G}\mid y_{j}=z\}.

{defi}

The
run language

\mathcal{R}(t)
of a KL term
t
is a set of runs with
\langle 1,1\rangle
-interface, defined as follows:

\displaystyle\mathcal{R}(a)

\displaystyle\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-3.0556pt\raisebox{5.64096pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\triangle$}}\hskip-3.0556pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\left\{\hbox to56.83pt{\vbox to6.67pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 14.18736pt\lower-3.33301pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke=#000000} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill=#000000} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width=0.4pt} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} \lxSVG@closescope \hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1}

We can also use the run languages as an alternative relational semantics.
Let
\mathfrak{A}
be a structure.
For
\vec{x},\vec{y}\in|\mathfrak{A}|^{*}
,
let
\tilde{\mathsf{G}}(\mathfrak{A},\vec{x},\vec{y})\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-3.0556pt\raisebox{5.64096pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\triangle$}}\hskip-3.0556pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\langle|\mathfrak{A}|,\{a^{\tilde{\mathsf{G}}(\mathfrak{A},\vec{x},\vec{y})}\}_{a\in\Sigma_{\mathtt{f},\mathtt{j}}},\vec{x},\vec{y}\rangle
where

a^{\tilde{\mathsf{G}}(\mathfrak{A},\vec{x},\vec{y})}=\llbracket a\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}\mbox{ for }a\in\Sigma

and

\mathtt{f}^{\tilde{\mathsf{G}}(\mathfrak{A},\vec{x},\vec{y})}=\mathtt{j}^{\tilde{\mathsf{G}}(\mathfrak{A},\vec{x},\vec{y})}=\{\langle z,z,z\rangle\mid z\in|\mathfrak{A}|\}
.

For a run
H
and a set
\mathcal{G}
of runs,
we define
\llbracket H\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}
and
\llbracket\mathcal{G}\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}
as follows:

\displaystyle\llbracket H\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}

\displaystyle\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-3.0556pt\raisebox{5.64096pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\triangle$}}\hskip-3.0556pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\{\vec{x}\vec{y}\mid\vec{x}\in|\mathfrak{A}|^{\mathrm{\mathop{ty}}_{1}(H)}\land\vec{y}\in|\mathfrak{A}|^{\mathrm{\mathop{ty}}_{2}(H)}\land H\longrightarrow\tilde{\mathsf{G}}(\mathfrak{A},\vec{x},\vec{y})\},

\displaystyle\llbracket\mathcal{G}\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-3.0556pt\raisebox{5.64096pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\triangle$}}\hskip-3.0556pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\bigcup_{H\in\mathcal{G}}\llbracket H\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}.

We then have the following as with
Section

2.1.2
.

Proposition 10
.

Let
\mathfrak{A}
be a structure.
For all KL terms
t
, we have
\llbracket t\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}=\llbracket\mathcal{R}(t)\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}
.

Proof 2.9
.

By easy induction on
t
using distributivity of
\mathbin{;}
and
\mathbin{\cap}
.

Every run can be expressed as series compositions of atomic runs.

Proposition 11
.

For every run
G
with
n\geq 1
edges,
there exist some
a_{1},\dots,a_{n}\in\bar{\Sigma}
such that
G=a_{1}\diamond\dots\diamond a_{n}
.

Proof 2.10
.

By easy induction on
n
.

This decomposition is not unique if the “topological sort of edges” of the run (i.e., the linear ordering of edges such that for every vertex, each incoming edge of the vertex comes before each outgoing edge of the vertex in the ordering) is not unique.
For instance,

\mathtt{f}^{1}_{1}\diamond b^{2}_{2}\diamond a^{2}_{1}\diamond c^{2}_{2}\diamond\mathtt{j}^{1}_{1}
and

\mathtt{f}^{1}_{1}\diamond b^{2}_{2}\diamond c^{2}_{2}\diamond a^{2}_{1}\diamond\mathtt{j}^{1}_{1}
also express the same run above.

2.2.3.
Left quotients of runs

For runs, we define
left quotients
with respect to series compositions.
For runs
G
,
H
, and
J
,
we write:

G\longrightarrow_{J}H\;\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 5.0pt\hskip-5.0pt\hbox{$\iff$}\hskip-5.0pt\hskip-3.0556pt\raisebox{5.64096pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\triangle$}}\hskip-3.0556pt\hskip 5.0pt}}\;\mbox{$J\diamond H$ is defined and }G=J\diamond H.

The
left quotient

\D_{J}(G)
of a run
G
with respect to a run
J
is the run language defined by:

\displaystyle\D_{J}(G)

\displaystyle\;\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-3.0556pt\raisebox{5.64096pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\triangle$}}\hskip-3.0556pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\;\{H\mid G\longrightarrow_{J}H\}.

For a run language
\mathcal{G}
, let
\D_{J}(\mathcal{G})\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-3.0556pt\raisebox{5.64096pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\triangle$}}\hskip-3.0556pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\bigcup_{G\in\mathcal{G}}\D_{J}(G)
.
For instance, when
J=\left(\hbox to75.3pt{\vbox to31.42pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 13.18735pt\lower-26.47182pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke=#000000} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill=#000000} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width=0.4pt} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} \lxSVG@closescope \hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1}
\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\hbox{\hbox{{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} {}{{}}{}{{}}

Let
n\in{\rm Nature}
.
For a run
G
,
the
emptiness property

\EPS_{n}(G)
is the truth value defined by:

\displaystyle\EPS_{n}(G)

\displaystyle\;\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-3.0556pt\raisebox{5.64096pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\triangle$}}\hskip-3.0556pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\;\begin{cases}\mathsf{true}&(G=\mathsf{1}^{n})\\
\mathsf{false}&(\mbox{otherwise}).\end{cases}

For a run language
\mathcal{G}
, let
\EPS_{n}(\mathcal{G})\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-3.0556pt\raisebox{5.64096pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\triangle$}}\hskip-3.0556pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\bigvee_{G\in\mathcal{G}}\EPS_{n}(G)
.
The following is clear by definition.

Proposition 12
.

For all runs
G
, we have
\EPS_{\mathrm{\mathop{ty}}_{2}(G)}(\D_{G}(G))
.

2.3.
Runs on structures

We also introduce
runs on structures
to simplify the use of the semantics using runs (
Proposition

10
).
Let
\mathfrak{A}
be a structure.
An
\mathfrak{A}
-run
with
\langle\vec{x},\vec{y}\rangle
-interface is a graph homomorphism
\tau\colon H\longrightarrow\tilde{\mathsf{G}}(\mathfrak{A},\vec{x},\vec{y})
, where
H
is some run.
We let
\mathrm{\mathop{ty}}(\tau)\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-3.0556pt\raisebox{5.64096pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\triangle$}}\hskip-3.0556pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\langle\mathrm{\mathop{ty}}_{\mathsf{1}}(\tau),\mathrm{\mathop{ty}}_{\mathsf{2}}(\tau)\rangle\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-3.0556pt\raisebox{5.64096pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\triangle$}}\hskip-3.0556pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\langle\vec{x},\vec{y}\rangle
.
We use
\tau,\sigma,\rho
to denote
\mathfrak{A}
-runs.
For brevity, we depict
\mathfrak{A}
-runs as vertex-labeled graphs where each vertex is labeled with a vertex of
\mathfrak{A}
.
For instance, let
\mathfrak{A}=\left(\hbox to39.39pt{\vbox to16.98pt{\pgfpicture\makeatletter\hbox{\hskip 5.2581pt\lower-8.9508pt\hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} \lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke=#000000} \lxSVG@begingroup@{fill=#000000} \lxSVG@setlinewidth{\the\pgflinewidth}\lxSVG@begingroup@{stroke-width=0.4pt} \lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\nullfont\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1} \lxSVG@closescope \hbox to0.0pt{\lxSVG@begingroup@{_scopebegin=1}

For two
\mathfrak{A}
-runs with
\langle\vec{x},\vec{y}\rangle
-interface,

\tau\colon H\longrightarrow\tilde{\mathsf{G}}(\mathfrak{A},\vec{x},\vec{y})

and
\sigma\colon J\longrightarrow\tilde{\mathsf{G}}(\mathfrak{A},\vec{x},\vec{y})
,
we say that a map
f\colon|H|\to|J|
is an
\mathfrak{A}
-run isomorphism
from
\tau
to
\sigma
, written
f\colon\tau\cong\sigma
, if

f\colon H\cong J\mbox{ and for all $x\in|H|$, $\tau(x)=\sigma(f(x))$}
.
We write
\tau\cong\sigma
if there is some
f
such that
f\colon\tau\cong\sigma
.
In the sequel, we identify two
\mathfrak{A}
-runs if there is an
\mathfrak{A}
-run isomorphism between them;
we write
\tau=\sigma
when
\tau\cong\sigma
.

For a KL term
t
and
x,y\in|\mathfrak{A}|
,
we write
\mathcal{R}^{\mathfrak{A}}_{x,y}(t)
for the
\mathfrak{A}
-run language defined by:

\mathcal{R}^{\mathfrak{A}}_{x,y}(t)\;\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-3.0556pt\raisebox{5.64096pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\triangle$}}\hskip-3.0556pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\;\{\tau\colon H\longrightarrow\tilde{\mathsf{G}}(\mathfrak{A},x,y)\mid H\in\mathcal{R}(t)\}.

Using
\mathfrak{A}
-runs, we can rephrase
Proposition

10
as follows.

Proposition 13
.

Let
\mathfrak{A}
be a structure.
For all KL term
t
,
we have:

\llbracket t\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}\;=\;\{\langle x,y\rangle\in|\mathfrak{A}|^{2}\mid\mathcal{R}^{\mathfrak{A}}_{x,y}(t)\neq\emptyset\}.

Proof 2.11
.

By easy induction on
t
(or an easy consequence of
Proposition

10
, as

\langle x,y\rangle\in\llbracket t\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}

iff
\exists H\in\mathcal{R}(t),\exists\tau,\tau\colon H\longrightarrow\tilde{\mathsf{G}}(\mathfrak{A},x,y)

iff
\mathcal{R}^{\mathfrak{A}}_{x,y}(t)\neq\emptyset
).

2.3.1.
Compositions on
\mathfrak{A}
-runs

We recall the series composition
\diamond
, the parallel composition
\parallel
, and the identity element
\mathsf{1}^{n}
(
Section

2
) for graphs with bi-interface.
Similarly, we define them also for
\mathfrak{A}
-runs.

{defi}

Let
\tau\colon H\longrightarrow\tilde{\mathsf{G}}(\mathfrak{A},\vec{x},\vec{y})
and

\sigma\colon J\longrightarrow\tilde{\mathsf{G}}(\mathfrak{A},\vec{x}^{\prime},\vec{y}^{\prime})
be
\mathfrak{A}
-runs.
Under
\vec{y}=\vec{x}^{\prime}
,
the
series composition

\tau\diamond\sigma\colon(H\diamond J)\longrightarrow\tilde{\mathsf{G}}(\mathfrak{A},\vec{x},\vec{y}^{\prime})
is defined (undefined when
\vec{y}\neq\vec{x}^{\prime}
) as the map such that,
for each vertex
x\in|H\diamond J|
,
if
x
is induced from a vertex
y\in|H|
,
then
(\tau\diamond\sigma)(x)=\tau(y)
,
and
if
x
is induced from a vertex
y\in|J|
,
then
(\tau\diamond\sigma)(x)=\sigma(y)
.
The
parallel composition

\tau\parallel\sigma\colon(H\parallel J)\longrightarrow\tilde{\mathsf{G}}(\mathfrak{A},\vec{x}\vec{x}^{\prime},\vec{y}\vec{y}^{\prime})

is defined as the map such that
if
x
is induced from a vertex
y\in|H|
,
then
(\tau\parallel\sigma)(x)=\tau(y)
,
and
if
x
is induced from a vertex
y\in|J|
,
then
(\tau\parallel\sigma)(x)=\sigma(y)
.
For each
\vec{x}=x_{1}\dots x_{n}\in|\mathfrak{A}|^{*}
,
let
\mathsf{1}^{\vec{x}}\colon\mathsf{1}^{n}\longrightarrow\tilde{\mathsf{G}}(\mathfrak{A},\vec{x},\vec{x})
be the
\mathfrak{A}
-run such that
for each
i\in[n]
, the
i
-th source/target vertex maps to
x_{i}
.

The left and right identity element with respect to
\diamond
on
\mathfrak{A}
-runs with
\langle\vec{x},\vec{y}\rangle
-interface are given by
\mathsf{1}^{\vec{x}}
and
\mathsf{1}^{\vec{y}}
, respectively, i.e.,
\mathsf{1}^{\vec{x}}\diamond\tau=\tau\diamond\mathsf{1}^{\vec{y}}=\tau
.
The identity element with respect to
\parallel
on
\mathfrak{A}
-runs with
\langle\vec{x},\vec{y}\rangle
-interface
is given by
\mathsf{1}^{\varepsilon}
, i.e.,
\mathsf{1}^{\varepsilon}\parallel\tau=\tau\parallel\mathsf{1}^{\varepsilon}=\tau
.

-runs

, is defined as
\bar{\Sigma}_{\mathfrak{A}}\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-3.0556pt\raisebox{5.64096pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\triangle$}}\hskip-3.0556pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\{a^{\vec{z},z^{\prime}}_{i}\mid a\in\Sigma,n\geq 1,i\in[n],\vec{z}\in|\mathfrak{A}|^{n},z^{\prime}\in|\mathfrak{A}|,\langle z_{i},z^{\prime}\rangle\in\llbracket a\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}\}\cup\{\mathtt{f}^{\vec{z}}_{i},\mathtt{j}^{\vec{z}}_{i}\mid n\geq 1,i\in[n],\vec{z}\in|\mathfrak{A}|^{n}\}
.
Every
\mathfrak{A}
-run can be expressed as series compositions of atomic
\mathfrak{A}
-runs, as follows (as with
Proposition

11
).

Proposition 14
.

Let
\mathfrak{A}
be a structure.
For every
\mathfrak{A}
-run
\tau
with
n\geq 1
edges,
there exist some
a_{1},\dots,a_{n}\in\bar{\Sigma}_{\mathfrak{A}}
such that
\tau=a_{1}\diamond\dots\diamond a_{n}
.

, we have

.
The decomposition of
\tau
is not unique, as

\mathtt{f}^{x}_{1}\diamond b^{xx,x}_{2}\diamond a^{xx,y}_{1}\diamond c^{yx,y}_{2}\diamond\mathtt{j}^{y}_{1}
and

\mathtt{f}^{x}_{1}\diamond b^{xx,x}_{2}\diamond c^{xx,y}_{2}\diamond a^{xy,y}_{1}\diamond\mathtt{j}^{y}_{1}

also express
\tau
.

2.3.2.
Left quotients of
\mathfrak{A}
-runs

Let
\mathfrak{A}
be a structure.
Similar to
Section

2.2.3
,
we define the left quotients and emptiness property for
\mathfrak{A}
-runs.
For
\mathfrak{A}
-runs
\tau
,
\sigma
, and
\rho
, we write:

\tau\longrightarrow^{\mathfrak{A}}_{\rho}\sigma\;\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 5.0pt\hskip-5.0pt\hbox{$\iff$}\hskip-5.0pt\hskip-3.0556pt\raisebox{5.64096pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\triangle$}}\hskip-3.0556pt\hskip 5.0pt}}\;\mbox{$\rho\diamond\sigma$ is defined and }\tau\cong\rho\diamond\sigma.

For
\mathfrak{A}
-runs
\tau
and
\rho
,
the
left quotient

\D^{\mathfrak{A}}_{\rho}(\tau)
of
\tau
with respect to
\rho

is the
\mathfrak{A}
-run language defined by:

\displaystyle\D^{\mathfrak{A}}_{\rho}(\tau)

\displaystyle\;\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-3.0556pt\raisebox{5.64096pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\triangle$}}\hskip-3.0556pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\;\{\sigma\mbox{ an $\mathfrak{A}$-run}\mid\tau\longrightarrow_{\rho}\sigma\}.

For an
\mathfrak{A}
-run language
\mathcal{G}
, let
\D^{\mathfrak{A}}_{\rho}(\mathcal{G})\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-3.0556pt\raisebox{5.64096pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\triangle$}}\hskip-3.0556pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\bigcup_{\tau\in\mathcal{G}}\D^{\mathfrak{A}}_{\rho}(\tau)
.

For an
\mathfrak{A}
-run
\tau
and
\vec{z}\in|\mathfrak{A}|^{*}
,
the
emptiness property

\EPS_{\vec{z}}(\tau)
is the truth value defined by:

\displaystyle\EPS_{\vec{z}}(\tau)

\displaystyle\;\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-3.0556pt\raisebox{5.64096pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\triangle$}}\hskip-3.0556pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\;\begin{cases}\mathsf{true}&(\tau=\mathsf{1}^{\vec{z}})\\
\mathsf{false}&(\mbox{otherwise}).\end{cases}

For an
\mathfrak{A}
-run language
\mathcal{G}
, let
\EPS_{\vec{z}}(\mathcal{G})\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-3.0556pt\raisebox{5.64096pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\triangle$}}\hskip-3.0556pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\bigvee_{\tau\in\mathcal{G}}\EPS_{\vec{z}}(\tau)
.
The following is clear by definition.

Proposition 15
.

Let
\mathfrak{A}
be a structure.
For all
\mathfrak{A}
-runs
\tau
,
we have
\EPS_{\mathrm{\mathop{ty}}_{2}(\tau)}(\D^{\mathfrak{A}}_{\tau}(\tau))
.

We will define derivatives based on these left quotient and emptiness property.

3.
Labeled Kleene Lattice Terms

To present derivatives (which will be used for an automata construction for PCoR*),
we consider simulating left quotients of
\mathfrak{A}
-runs (
Section

2.3.2
) by terms.
To this end, we extend the syntax of terms with “labels”.
In a nutshell, labels are used for expressing runs with
multiple
source vertices.

Let
L
be a set of
labels
.
We use
x,y,z
to denote labels.
The set of
labeled Kleene lattice terms
(lKL terms) is defined by the following grammar:

\displaystyle\tilde{t},\tilde{s},\tilde{{u}}\in\tilde{\mathbf{T}}_{L}

\displaystyle\;\Coloneqq\;@x.t\mid\tilde{t}\mathbin{;}_{1}s\mid\tilde{t}\mathbin{\cap}_{1}\tilde{s}\qquad

(
x\in L
and
t,s
are KL terms)

Each label
x
indicates the vertex
x
on a structure (if exists).
The notation
@x.t
is inspired by the jump operator in hybrid logics
[
arecesHybridLogics2007
]
(a minor difference is that
x
directly indicates a vertex name, here).
We explicitly use
\mathbin{;}_{1}
and
\mathbin{\cap}_{1}
instead of
\mathbin{;}
and
\mathbin{\cap}
in lKL terms,
as labeled terms interpret unary relations (
cf.

Section

3.1
).
We write
\mathsf{lab}_{i}(\tilde{t})
for the
i
-th label occurring in
\tilde{t}
,
and we write
\overrightarrow{\mathsf{lab}}(\tilde{t})
for the sequence
\mathsf{lab}_{1}(\tilde{t})\dots\mathsf{lab}_{n}(\tilde{t})
where

n
is the number of labels occurring in
\tilde{t}
.
For instance, if
\tilde{t}=((@x.\tilde{s}_{1})\mathbin{\cap}_{1}(((@x.\tilde{s}_{2})\mathbin{\cap}_{1}(@y.\tilde{s}_{3}))\mathbin{;}_{1}{u}_{1}))\mathbin{;}_{1}{u}_{2}
,
then
\mathsf{lab}_{1}(\tilde{t})=x
,
\mathsf{lab}_{2}(\tilde{t})=x
,
\mathsf{lab}_{3}(\tilde{t})=y
, and

\overrightarrow{\mathsf{lab}}(\tilde{t})=xxy
.

3.1.
Semantics: relational models

Let
\mathfrak{A}\in\mathsf{REL}
.
For an lKL term
\tilde{t}
,
the
semantics

\llbracket\tilde{t}\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}\subseteq|\mathfrak{A}|
is a unary relation defined as follows:

\displaystyle\llbracket @x.t\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}

\displaystyle\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-3.0556pt\raisebox{5.64096pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\triangle$}}\hskip-3.0556pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\{y\mid\langle x,y\rangle\in\llbracket t\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}\},

\displaystyle\hskip-6.99997pt\llbracket\tilde{t}\mathbin{;}_{1}s\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}

\displaystyle\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-3.0556pt\raisebox{5.64096pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\triangle$}}\hskip-3.0556pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\{z\mid y\in\llbracket\tilde{t}\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}},\langle y,z\rangle\in\llbracket s\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}\},

\displaystyle\hskip-6.99997pt\llbracket\tilde{t}\mathbin{\cap}_{1}\tilde{s}\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}

\displaystyle\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-3.0556pt\raisebox{5.64096pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\triangle$}}\hskip-3.0556pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\llbracket\tilde{t}\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}\cap\llbracket\tilde{s}\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}.

Note that
\llbracket @x.t\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}=\emptyset
when
x\not\in|\mathfrak{A}|
.
Also, note that
\llbracket t\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}
is a
binary
relation for KL terms
t

and
\llbracket\tilde{t}\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}
is a
unary
relation for lKL terms
\tilde{t}
.
For
\mathcal{C}\subseteq\mathsf{REL}
,
we write
\mathcal{C}\models\tilde{t}=\tilde{s}
if
\llbracket\tilde{t}\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}=\llbracket\tilde{s}\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}
for
\mathfrak{A}\in\mathcal{C}
.
We then have the following easy fact.

Proposition 16
.

Let
t
and
s
be KL terms and
x
be a label.
We then have:

\mathsf{REL}\models t\leq s\;\iff\;\mathsf{REL}\models @x.t\leq @x.s.

Proof 3.1
.

(
\Longrightarrow
):
Trivial.
(
\Longleftarrow
):
Let
\langle y,z\rangle\in\llbracket t\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}
.
Let
f
and
\mathfrak{B}
be such that
f\colon\mathfrak{A}\cong\mathfrak{B}
and
f(y)=x
.
We then have that for all KL terms
{u}
,

\langle y,z\rangle\in\llbracket{u}\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}

iff
\langle x,f(z)\rangle\in\llbracket{u}\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{B}}
(since
\mathfrak{A}\cong\mathfrak{B}
and
{u}
is a (non-labelled) KL term)
iff
f(z)\in\llbracket @x.{u}\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{B}}
(by the definition of
\llbracket\_\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{B}}
).
We thus have
f(z)\in\llbracket @x.t\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}
.
By the assumption,

f(z)\in\llbracket @x.s\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{B}}
.
Hence, by the reverse direction of the above argument,
we have
\langle y,z\rangle\in\llbracket s\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}
.

Note that for labeled KL terms
\tilde{t}
,
\llbracket\tilde{t}\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}
and
\llbracket\tilde{t}\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{B}}
may not be equal even if
\mathfrak{A}\cong\mathfrak{B}
, because we use the names of vertices in the semantics (
cf.
nominals in hybrid logic
[
arecesHybridLogics2007
]
).
For that reason, for structures, we distinguish two structures even if they are isomorphic,
cf.
we identify two graphs/runs/
\mathfrak{A}
-runs if they are isomorphic.

3.2.
Runs on structures

We use the following notation:

X\mathop{\heartsuit}Y\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-3.0556pt\raisebox{5.64096pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\triangle$}}\hskip-3.0556pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\{\tau\mathop{\heartsuit}\sigma\mid\tau\in X\land\sigma\in Y\}

where
X
and
Y
are sets of runs or sets of
\mathfrak{A}
-runs and
\mathop{\heartsuit}\in\{\diamond,\parallel\}
.
In this set notation, we use terms as singleton sets: for instance,
\{\tau,\sigma\}\diamond\rho=\{\tau\diamond\rho,\sigma\diamond\rho\}
.

{defi}

Let
\mathfrak{A}
be a structure.
For an lKL term
\tilde{t}
and
z\in|\mathfrak{A}|
,
the
\mathfrak{A}
-run language

\mathcal{R}^{\mathfrak{A}}_{z}(\tilde{t})
is defined as follows:

\displaystyle\mathcal{R}^{\mathfrak{A}}_{z}(@x.t)

\displaystyle\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-3.0556pt\raisebox{5.64096pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\triangle$}}\hskip-3.0556pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\mathcal{R}^{\mathfrak{A}}_{x,z}(t),

\displaystyle\hskip-5.0pt\mathcal{R}^{\mathfrak{A}}_{z}(\tilde{t}\mathbin{;}_{1}s)

\displaystyle\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-3.0556pt\raisebox{5.64096pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\triangle$}}\hskip-3.0556pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\bigcup_{y\in|\mathfrak{A}|}\mathcal{R}^{\mathfrak{A}}_{y}(\tilde{t})\diamond\mathcal{R}^{\mathfrak{A}}_{y,z}(s),

\displaystyle\hskip-5.0pt\mathcal{R}^{\mathfrak{A}}_{z}(\tilde{t}\mathbin{\cap}_{1}\tilde{s})

\displaystyle\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-3.0556pt\raisebox{5.64096pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\triangle$}}\hskip-3.0556pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}(\mathcal{R}^{\mathfrak{A}}_{z}(\tilde{t})\parallel\mathcal{R}^{\mathfrak{A}}_{z}(\tilde{s}))\diamond\mathtt{j}_{1}^{z}.

Proposition 17

(
cf.

Proposition

13
)
.

Let
\mathfrak{A}
be a structure.
For all lKL term
\tilde{t}
,
we have:

\llbracket\tilde{t}\rrbracket_{\mathfrak{A}}\;=\;\{z\in|\mathfrak{A}|\mid\mathcal{R}^{\mathfrak{A}}_{z}(\tilde{t})\neq\emptyset\}.

Proof 3.2
.

By easy induction on
\tilde{t}
using
Proposition

13
.

4.
Derivatives on Graphs

We recall the left quotients of
\mathfrak{A}
-runs (defined in
Section

2.3.2
).
In this section, we now define derivatives on
\mathfrak{A}
, which can simulate the left quotients.
We first define the emptiness property in the term level (
Section

4
), and then define the derivatives on graphs (
Sections

4
and
), based on derivatives on strings
[
brzozowskiDerivativesRegularExpressions1964
,
antimirovPartialDerivativesRegular1996
,
sakarovitchElementsAutomataTheory2009
]
.

{defi}

For a label
z
and an lKL term
\tilde{t}
,
the truth value
\EPS_{z}(\tilde{t})\in\{\mathsf{false},\mathsf{true}\}
is defined as follows:
2
2

2

The definition
\EPS_{z}(@x.s\mathbin{\cap}{u})\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-3.0556pt\raisebox{5.64096pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\triangle$}}\hskip-3.0556pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\EPS_{z}(\tilde{s}\mathbin{\cap}_{1}\tilde{{u}})\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-3.0556pt\raisebox{5.64096pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\triangle$}}\hskip-3.0556pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\mathsf{false}
is due to that each
\mathfrak{A}
-run of
\mathcal{R}^{\mathfrak{A}}_{z}(@x.s\mathbin{\cap}{u})
and
\mathcal{R}^{\mathfrak{A}}_{z}(\tilde{s}\mathbin{\cap}_{1}\tilde{{u}})
always contains
\mathtt{j}^{z}_{1}
(
Section

3.2
), so they do not contain the run having the emptiness property.

\displaystyle\EPS_{z}(@x.a)

\displaystyle\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-3.0556pt\raisebox{5.64096pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\triangle$}}\hskip-3.0556pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\EPS_{z}(@x.\mathsf{0})\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-3.0556pt\raisebox{5.64096pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\triangle$}}\hskip-3.0556pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\EPS_{z}(@x.s\mathbin{\cap}{u})\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-3.0556pt\raisebox{5.64096pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\triangle$}}\hskip-3.0556pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\EPS_{z}(\tilde{s}\mathbin{\cap}_{1}\tilde{{u}})\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-3.0556pt\raisebox{5.64096pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\triangle$}}\hskip-3.0556pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\mathsf{false},

\displaystyle\EPS_{z}(@x.\mathsf{1})

\displaystyle\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-3.0556pt\raisebox{5.64096pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\triangle$}}\hskip-3.0556pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\EPS_{z}(@x.s^{*})\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-3.0556pt\raisebox{5.64096pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\triangle$}}\hskip-3.0556pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\begin{cases}\mathsf{true}&(x=z)\\
\mathsf{false}&(x\neq z),\end{cases}

\displaystyle\EPS_{z}(\tilde{s}\mathbin{;}_{1}{u})

\displaystyle\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-3.0556pt\raisebox{5.64096pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\triangle$}}\hskip-3.0556pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\EPS_{z}(\tilde{s})\land\EPS_{z}(@z.{u}),

\displaystyle\EPS_{z}(@x.s\mathbin{;}{u})

\displaystyle\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-3.0556pt\raisebox{5.64096pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\triangle$}}\hskip-3.0556pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\EPS_{z}(@x.s)\land\EPS_{z}(@z.{u}),

\displaystyle\EPS_{z}(@x.s\mathbin{+}{u})

\displaystyle\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-3.0556pt\raisebox{5.64096pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\triangle$}}\hskip-3.0556pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\EPS_{z}(@x.s)\lor\EPS_{z}(@x.{u}).

For a label
z
and a set
\tilde{T}
of lKL terms, let
\EPS_{z}(\tilde{T})\mathrel{\hbox{\hskip 3.8889pt\hskip-3.8889pt\hbox{$=$}\hskip-3.8889pt\hskip-3.0556pt\raisebox{5.64096pt}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\triangle$}}\hskip-3.0556pt\hskip 3.8889pt}}\bigvee_{\tilde{t}\in\tilde{T}}\EPS_{z}(\tilde{t})
.
This
\EPS_{z}
(
Section

4
) is defined so that we can encode the emptiness property
\EPS_{z}
(in
Section

2.2.3
) as follows.

Lemma 18
.

Let
\mathfrak{A}
be a structure.
For all
z\in|\mathfrak{A}|
and lKL terms
\tilde{t}
,
we have:

\EPS_{z}(\mathcal{R}^{\mathfrak{A}}_{z}(\tilde{t}))\;\iff\;\EPS_{z}(\tilde{t}).

Proof 4.1
.

By easy induction on
\tilde{t}
, with unfolding the definitions.

•

Case
\tilde{t}=@x.a,@x.\mathsf{0},@x.s\mathbin{\cap}{u},\tilde{s}\mathbin{\cap}_{1}\tilde{{u}}
:
By
\EPS_{z}(\mathcal{R}^{\mathfrak{A}}_{z}(\tilde{t}))
iff
\mathsf{false}
.

•

Case
\tilde{t}=@x.\mathsf{1},@x.s^{*}
:
By
\EPS_{z}(\mathcal{R}^{\mathfrak{A}}_{z}(\tilde{t}))
iff
\begin{cases}\mathsf{true}&(x=z)\\
\mathsf{false}&(x\neq z).\end{cases}

•

Case
\tilde{t}=@x.s\mathbin{;}{u}
:
We have:

\displaystyle\EPS_{z}(\mathcal{R}^{\mathfrak{A}}_{z}(@x.s\mathbin{;}{u}))

\displaystyle\;\iff\;\EPS_{z}(\bigcup_{y\in|\mathfrak{A}|}\mathcal{R}^{\mathfrak{A}}_{y}(@x.s)\diamond\mathcal{R}^{\mathfrak{A}}_{z}(@y.{u}))

(
Section

3.2
of
\mathcal{R}^{\mathfrak{A}}_{z}
)

\displaystyle\;\iff\;\bigvee_{y\in|\mathfrak{A}|}\EPS_{y}(\mathcal{R}^{\mathfrak{A}}_{z}(@x.s))\land\EPS_{z}(\mathcal{R}^{\mathfrak{A}}_{z}(@y.{u}))

(By
\EPS_{z}(\tau\diamond\sigma)
iff
\EPS_{z}(\tau)\land\EPS_{z}(\sigma)
)

\displaystyle\;\iff\;\EPS_{z}(\mathcal{R}^{\mathfrak{A}}_{z}(@x.s))\land\EPS_{z}(\mathcal{R}^{\mathfrak{A}}_{z}(@z.{u}))

(
\EPS_{y}(\mathcal{R}^{\mathfrak{A}}_{z}(@x.s))
is
\mathsf{false}
when
y\neq z
)

\displaystyle\;\iff\;\EPS_{z}(@x.s)\land\EPS_{z}(@z.{u})

(IH)

\displaystyle\;\iff\;\EPS_{z}(@x.s\mathbin{;}{u}).

(
Section

4
)

•

Case
\tilde{t}=\tilde{s}\mathbin{;}_{1}{u}
:
Similar to the case above.

•

Case
\tilde{t}=@x.s\mathbin{+}{u}
:
We have:

\displaystyle\EPS_{z}(\mathcal{R}^{\mathfrak{A}}_{z}(@x.s\mathbin{+}{u}))

\displaystyle\;\iff\;\EPS_{z}(\mathcal{R}^{\mathfrak{A}}_{z}(@x.s)\cup\mathcal{R}^{\mathfrak{A}}_{z}(@z.{u}))

(
Section

3.2
of
\mathcal{R}^{\mathfrak{A}}_{z}
)

\displaystyle\;\iff\;\EPS_{z}(\mathcal{R}^{\mathfrak{A}}_{z}(@x.s))\lor\EPS_{z}(\mathcal{R}^{\mathfrak{A}}_{z}(@z.{u}))

(By
\EPS_{z}(\mathcal{G})=\bigvee_{\tau\in\mathcal{G}}\EPS_{z}(\tau)
)

\displaystyle\;\iff\;\EPS_{z}(@x.s)\lor\EPS_{z}(@z.{u})

(IH)

\displaystyle\;\iff\;\EPS_{z}(@x.s\mathbin{+}{u}).

(
Section

4
)

Hence, this completes the proof.

{defi}

Let
\mathfrak{A}
be a structure.
The
derivative
relation
\tilde{t}\longrightarrow^{\mathfrak{A}}_{\rho}\tilde{s}
,
where
\tilde{t}
and
\tilde{s}
are lKL terms and
\rho
is an
\mathfrak{A}
-run,
is defined as the smallest relation (of tuples of
\tilde{t}
,
\tilde{s}
, and
\rho
) closed under the following rules:
